pos: n. (a high priest in the line of Eleazar; also a Levite overseer after the return)
etymology: Hebrew Uzzi, meaning my strength, from oz, strength. Several men bear it; the chief is a link in the unbroken priestly descent from Aaron through Eleazar.
biblical_def: The Chronicler traces the high-priestly succession name by name, and Uzzi stands in the middle of it: “And Abishua begat Bukki, and Bukki begat Uzzi” (1 Chronicles 6:5), and the line continues, “And Uzzi begat Zerahiah, and Zerahiah begat Meraioth” (1 Chronicles 6:6). The same descent is given again in the register of those who ministered before the dwelling place: “Bukki his son, Uzzi his son, Zerahiah his son” (1 Chronicles 6:51). The whole point of such a list is stated where it begins: the priesthood was not an office a man entered by aptitude or ambition but one he was born into, in a line God fixed at Sinai. Another Uzzi appears among those who returned from Babylon, set over the Levites in Jerusalem: “The overseer also of the Levites at Jerusalem was Uzzi the son of Bani, the son of Hashabiah, the son of Mattaniah, the son of Micha. Of the sons of Asaph, the singers were over the business of the house of God” (Nehemiah 11:22). Names like this one are the connective tissue of the Old Testament's central claim about worship: that God appointed who should draw near, and kept the record.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Uzzi; the Hebrew signifies my strength, and the name belongs to a high priest of Aaron's line and to several others.
webster_full: UZZI, n. A descendant of Aaron through Eleazar, in the line of the high priests; in Hebrew, my strength.
SUCCESSION, n. A following of one thing after another; the order of one person succeeding another in office.
PRIESTHOOD, n. The office or character of a priest; the order of men set apart for sacred offices.
OVERSEER, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; a supervisor.
LINEAL, a. Composed of lines; descending in a direct line from an ancestor.
scriptures: And Abishua begat Bukki, and Bukki begat Uzzi,
And Uzzi begat Zerahiah, and Zerahiah begat Meraioth,
Bukki his son, Uzzi his son, Zerahiah his son,

The overseer also of the Levites at Jerusalem was Uzzi the son of Bani, the son of Hashabiah, the son of Mattaniah, the son of Micha. Of the sons of Asaph, the singers were over the business of the house of God.
corruption_summary: Ordination is treated as a matter of gifting and self-assessment, against a canon that takes pains to record who was appointed and by what descent.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that access to God has never been self-authorised. The Aaronic line is recorded generation by generation precisely because no Israelite could appoint himself to it; Korah tried and was swallowed, Saul offered sacrifice and lost his kingdom, and Uzziah burned incense and went out a leper. The lists of Bukki and Uzzi and Zerahiah are tedious to read and were indispensable to Israel, because they answered the only question that mattered at the altar: by what right does this man stand here?

The New Testament does not abolish the principle but fulfils it. Hebrews argues at length that Christ did not glorify Himself to be made an high priest but was called of God, and that His priesthood rests on the power of an endless life rather than on a genealogy. From that follows both the priesthood of all believers and the insistence, kept by the Reformed churches, that no man takes the office of elder to himself: he is tried, found blameless, and set apart by the church with the laying on of hands. Gift without calling is Korah's censer.

pos: n. (chief of the Kohathites; also a prince of Zebulun)
etymology: Hebrew Elitsaphan, meaning God hath protected or hidden. Two men bear it — the Levite who carried the sanctuary's holiest furniture, and a tribal prince appointed to divide the land.
biblical_def: The Kohathites bore the ark, the table, the candlestick and the altars, and their chief is named: “And the chief of the house of the father of the families of the Kohathites shall be Elizaphan the son of Uzziel” (Numbers 3:30). This is the man Moses called, with his brother Mishael, to carry the bodies of Nadab and Abihu out of the camp after strange fire. A second Elizaphan is set over the division of Canaan: “And the prince of the tribe of the children of Zebulun, Elizaphan the son of Parnach” (Numbers 34:25). The Levite's house reappears when David brings the ark to Jerusalem the second time, by the due order: “Of the sons of Elizaphan; Shemaiah the chief, and his brethren two hundred” (1 Chronicles 15:8). And the reason David summoned these families rather than hiring a cart is stated in the same chapter: “Then David said, None ought to carry the ark of God but the Levites: for them hath the LORD chosen to carry the ark of God, and to minister unto him for ever” (1 Chronicles 15:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Elizaphan; the Hebrew signifies God hath protected, and the name belongs to a Kohathite chief and to a prince of Zebulun.
webster_full: ELIZAPHAN, n. The son of Uzziel, chief of the Kohathites; in Hebrew, God hath protected.
KOHATHITES, n. The family of Levites descended from Kohath, charged with the most holy furniture of the sanctuary.
BEAR, v.t. To carry; to support and remove from place to place; to convey.
STAVES, n. plu. The poles by which the ark and other sacred vessels were borne upon the shoulders.
SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; the most retired and holy part of the temple or tabernacle.
scriptures: And the chief of the house of the father of the families of the Kohathites shall be Elizaphan the son of Uzziel.
And the prince of the tribe of the children of Zebulun, Elizaphan the son of Parnach.
Of the sons of Elizaphan; Shemaiah the chief, and his brethren two hundred:
Then David said, None ought to carry the ark of God but the Levites: for them hath the LORD chosen to carry the ark of God, and to minister unto him for ever.
corruption_summary: The care Scripture takes over who may handle holy things is treated as ritual fussiness, and David's own explanation of the breach at Perez-uzzah is passed over.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God appointed both the thing to be done and the persons to do it. The Kohathites under Elizaphan carried the ark on staves upon their shoulders; they were forbidden to touch the holy things or even to look upon them uncovered, on pain of death. When David first moved the ark he used a new cart, which was the Philistine method, and Uzzah died. Three months later he summoned the Levites, and named the sons of Elizaphan among them, saying plainly that none ought to carry the ark of God but the Levites.

The lesson David drew is the sentence that gave the Reformed churches their doctrine of worship: we sought him not after the due order. The first attempt had every mark of sincerity — thirty thousand chosen men, singing, harps, psalteries, cymbals, and a brand-new cart. What it lacked was obedience to a command already given. The question Scripture puts to any act of worship is not whether it is heartfelt or impressive but whether it is commanded, and Elizaphan's sons on the day of the second attempt are the picture of the right answer.

pos: n. (a Levite singer appointed to the ark; also a teaching Levite under Jehoshaphat)
etymology: Hebrew Shemiramoth, of uncertain meaning. The name belongs to one of the musicians David set before the ark, and to a Levite sent through Judah with the book of the law.
biblical_def: When David brought the ark to Jerusalem he appointed a permanent order of music, and this man is in every list of it. First among the second degree of singers: “And with them their brethren of the second degree, Zechariah, Ben, and Jaaziel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Unni, Eliab, and Benaiah, and Maaseiah, and Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, the porters” (1 Chronicles 15:18). Then with his instrument specified: “And Zechariah, and Aziel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Unni, and Eliab, and Maaseiah, and Benaiah, with psalteries on Alamoth” (1 Chronicles 15:20). And in the standing establishment before the ark: “Asaph the chief, and next to him Zechariah, Jeiel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Mattithiah, and Eliab, and Benaiah, and Obededom: and Jeiel with psalteries and with harps; but Asaph made a sound with cymbals” (1 Chronicles 16:5). Generations later a Levite of the same name is sent out on a very different errand: “And with them he sent Levites, even Shemaiah, and Nethaniah, and Zebadiah, and Asahel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehonathan, and Adonijah, and Tobijah, and Tobadonijah, Levites; and with them Elishama and Jehoram, priests” (2 Chronicles 17:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Shemiramoth; the name belongs to a Levite musician appointed by David and to a teaching Levite under Jehoshaphat.
webster_full: SHEMIRAMOTH, n. A Levite appointed by David among the singers before the ark.
PSALTERY, n. An instrument of music used by the Hebrews, the form of which is not certainly known.
ALAMOTH, n. A term in the titles of psalms and in Chronicles, understood of virgins' voices or a treble key.
CHORISTER, n. A singer in a concert; one who leads a choir in church music.
INSTRUCT, v.t. To teach; to inform the mind; to communicate knowledge to.
scriptures: And with them their brethren of the second degree, Zechariah, Ben, and Jaaziel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Unni, Eliab, and Benaiah, and Maaseiah, and Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, the porters.
And Zechariah, and Aziel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Unni, and Eliab, and Maaseiah, and Benaiah, with psalteries on Alamoth;

Asaph the chief, and next to him Zechariah, Jeiel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Mattithiah, and Eliab, and Benaiah, and Obededom: and Jeiel with psalteries and with harps; but Asaph made a sound with cymbals;

And with them he sent Levites, even Shemaiah, and Nethaniah, and Zebadiah, and Asahel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehonathan, and Adonijah, and Tobijah, and Tobadonijah, Levites; and with them Elishama and Jehoram, priests.
corruption_summary: Music in worship is treated as a matter of preference and effect, against a record in which the singers were named, appointed, trained and assigned by instrument.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how seriously Israel took the ordering of sung praise. Chronicles does not say that David arranged for music; it names the men, ranks them by degree, assigns instruments, specifies the key, and appoints Chenaniah as master of the song because he was skilful. Four thousand Levites praised the LORD with instruments David made for that purpose. This is neither casual nor improvised, and it is the background against which the New Testament commands psalms and hymns and spiritual songs.

The second Shemiramoth points to something equally worth noting. Jehoshaphat sent Levites through the cities of Judah with the book of the law to teach the people, and the reform that followed came from that teaching. The same order of men who sang before the ark carried the Scriptures into the towns. Worship and instruction were not rival departments in Israel and are not in the church; the Reformed insistence that singing be filled with the word, and that the ministry of the word govern the service, keeps the two in the relation Chronicles assumes.

pos: n. (a Levite musician under David; also a Levite of the return)
etymology: Hebrew Unni, perhaps meaning afflicted, from anah, to afflict. It belongs to a singer in David's choir and to a Levite who kept watch after the exile.
biblical_def: He is listed among the second rank of singers appointed when the ark came up: “And with them their brethren of the second degree, Zechariah, Ben, and Jaaziel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Unni, Eliab, and Benaiah, and Maaseiah, and Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, the porters” (1 Chronicles 15:18), and again with his instrument named: “And Zechariah, and Aziel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Unni, and Eliab, and Maaseiah, and Benaiah, with psalteries on Alamoth” (1 Chronicles 15:20). Centuries later a Levite of the same name stands in the restored order of service: “Also Bakbukiah and Unni, their brethren, were over against them in the watches” (Nehemiah 12:9). The watches were the appointed courses of praise, one company answering another. The arrangement had been David's: “And he appointed certain of the Levites to minister before the ark of the LORD, and to record, and to thank and praise the LORD God of Israel” (1 Chronicles 16:4). What was set up before the ark in Jerusalem was still being kept, by men standing over against one another, after the return from Babylon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Unni; the name belongs to a Levite singer appointed by David, and to a Levite in the courses after the captivity.
webster_full: UNNI, n. A Levite of the second degree among the singers appointed by David.
WATCH, n. A division of time appointed for keeping guard or for service; the period of duty.
COURSE, n. The order of succession in which the priests and Levites served in their turns.
ANTIPHONAL, a. Sung alternately by two choirs, one answering the other.
MINISTER, v.i. To attend and serve; to perform service in any office, sacred or secular.
scriptures: And with them their brethren of the second degree, Zechariah, Ben, and Jaaziel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Unni, Eliab, and Benaiah, and Maaseiah, and Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, the porters.
And Zechariah, and Aziel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Unni, and Eliab, and Maaseiah, and Benaiah, with psalteries on Alamoth;
Also Bakbukiah and Unni, their brethren, were over against them in the watches.
And he appointed certain of the Levites to minister before the ark of the LORD, and to record, and to thank and praise the LORD God of Israel:
corruption_summary: Continuity in worship is treated as mere tradition, when Scripture presents an order set up before the ark and still kept by name five centuries later.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the value Scripture places on continuity. David appointed certain Levites to minister before the ark, to record, and to thank and praise the LORD; that arrangement survived the division of the kingdom, the apostasy of successive reigns, the destruction of the temple, and seventy years of exile, and Nehemiah found men still standing in the watches, over against their brethren. Nothing in the record suggests the arrangement was preserved by enthusiasm. It was preserved because it had been appointed and men kept it.

A generation inclined to treat inherited forms as dead weight should weigh that. The Reformed churches have never held that antiquity makes a practice binding — Scripture alone binds the conscience, and the Reformation set aside a great deal of very ancient practice on that ground. But they have also refused the opposite error, which mistakes novelty for life. An order of worship handed down, tested against the word, and kept faithfully by men whose names appear once in a list is not lifeless. It is how the praise of God has usually travelled from one century to the next.

pos: n. (head of a family of Nethinims, and their overseer in Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Tsicha, of uncertain meaning. The name heads the list of the Nethinims — the given ones, temple servants assigned to the Levites for the menial work of the house of God.
biblical_def: When the exiles were numbered, a whole class of temple servants was counted, and this family stands first: “The Nethinims: the children of Ziha, the children of Hasupha, the children of Tabbaoth” (Ezra 2:43). Nehemiah's parallel register gives the same order: “The Nethinims: the children of Ziha, the children of Hashupha, the children of Tabbaoth” (Nehemiah 7:46). And when Jerusalem was resettled, the Nethinims were given a quarter and a head: “But the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel: and Ziha and Gispa were over the Nethinims” (Nehemiah 11:21). Their origin lies in David's reign and earlier — given, as the name says, to the service of the house: “Moreover David and the captains of the host separated to the service of the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who should prophesy with harps, with psalteries, and with cymbals” (1 Chronicles 25:1). The Nethinims did none of that. They drew water and cut wood and carried what needed carrying, and Ezra sent for some of them when he found no Levites among his returning company, because the house could not be served without them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Nethinim as servants of the priests and Levites, appointed to the meanest offices about the temple; Ziha is a head of that order.
webster_full: NETHINIM, n. plu. Servants given to the Levites for the inferior offices of the temple; the given ones.
ZIHA, n. The head of a family of the Nethinims, and an overseer of that order in Jerusalem.
OPHEL, n. A part of the hill of Zion at Jerusalem, where the Nethinims dwelt.
MENIAL, a. Pertaining to servants; low; mean; belonging to the humblest offices.
DEVOTE, v.t. To appropriate by vow; to set apart or dedicate by a solemn act; to consecrate.
scriptures: The Nethinims: the children of Ziha, the children of Hasupha, the children of Tabbaoth,
The Nethinims: the children of Ziha, the children of Hashupha, the children of Tabbaoth,
But the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel: and Ziha and Gispa were over the Nethinims.

Moreover David and the captains of the host separated to the service of the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who should prophesy with harps, with psalteries, and with cymbals: and the number of the workmen according to their service was:
corruption_summary: Humble service is ranked below visible ministry, and a class of men Scripture counts by name and settles by neighbourhood is treated as beneath notice.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the house of God ran on labour nobody watched. The Nethinims — the word means the given ones — cut the wood and drew the water. They did not sing, teach, or offer. And Scripture counts them family by family in two separate registers, names their chief, and records the street they lived on. Ezra, gathering his caravan for the return, discovered he had priests and no Levites, sent back for ministers for the house, and came away with two hundred and twenty Nethinims, every one of whom, he says, was expressed by name.

The gospel takes that valuation and deepens it. Our Lord washed feet and said that he that is greatest among you shall be your servant; Paul insists that the members of the body which seem to be more feeble are necessary, and that God has given more abundant honour to the part that lacked. A church that ranks its members by visibility has adopted a scale the Bible nowhere uses. The man who unlocks the building is in the same register as the man who preaches in it, and in Nehemiah's case the register survives and the sermon does not.

pos: n. (a chief of Manasseh; also a Benjamite and a Levitical house)
etymology: Hebrew Hodavyah, meaning praise ye the LORD, from hod, splendour or thanksgiving, with the divine name. The name is a sentence of praise carried by three different men.
biblical_def: A man of this name heads a house in the trans-Jordan tribes: “And these were the heads of the house of their fathers, even Epher, and Ishi, and Eliel, and Azriel, and Jeremiah, and Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty men of valour, famous men, and heads of the house of their fathers” (1 Chronicles 5:24). The verses immediately following record what became of that whole company, and the Chronicler does not soften it: they transgressed against the God of their fathers and went a whoring after the gods of the people of the land, and God stirred up the spirit of the king of Assyria and carried them away. A second bearer appears in Benjamin's register: “And of the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Hodaviah, the son of Hasenuah” (1 Chronicles 9:7). A third gives his name to a Levitical house that came back from Babylon: “The Levites: the children of Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the children of Hodaviah, seventy and four” (Ezra 2:40). Seventy-four Levites returned out of a nation. The number is small, and the name over them means praise ye the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Hodaviah; the Hebrew signifies praise ye the LORD, and the name belongs to three men in the genealogies.
webster_full: HODAVIAH, n. A head of a house in Manasseh; in Hebrew, praise ye the LORD.
VALOUR, n. Strength of mind in regard to danger; courage; intrepidity; prowess.
FAMOUS, a. Celebrated in fame or public report; renowned; much talked of and praised.
APOSTASY, n. An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith.
REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
scriptures: And these were the heads of the house of their fathers, even Epher, and Ishi, and Eliel, and Azriel, and Jeremiah, and Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty men of valour, famous men, and heads of the house of their fathers.
And of the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Hodaviah, the son of Hasenuah,
The Levites: the children of Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the children of Hodaviah, seventy and four.
And they transgressed against the God of their fathers, and went a whoring after the gods of the people of the land, whom God destroyed before them.
corruption_summary: Reputation is mistaken for standing before God, though the Chronicler applies the words famous and mighty to the very men he is about to record as apostates.
corruption_paragraphs: The sentence is one of the most deliberately arranged in Chronicles. Seven men are named as mighty men of valour, famous men, heads of the house of their fathers — every honour a tribe could confer — and the next verse begins, and they transgressed against the God of their fathers. The Chronicler does not withdraw the honours; he lets them stand and then records the apostasy, so the reader feels the distance between what men were called and what they were. Fame, capability and inherited position are all real and none of them is standing before God.

The name itself faces no postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pattern of the remnant. The house of Hodaviah in Manasseh went into Assyrian exile and out of the record; the house of Hodaviah among the Levites came back from Babylon, seventy-four men. Ezra counted more than forty thousand returning, and among them fewer than a hundred Levites of that house — a thin thread, and enough. God has never preserved His people by their numbers or their reputation, and the name over the small company is an imperative: praise ye the LORD.

pos: n. (a Levite who helped the people understand the law)
etymology: Hebrew Shabbethay, from shabbath, the sabbath — probably a name given to a child born on that day. He appears three times, always in the work of teaching or ordering the house of God.
biblical_def: He is first named among the men assigned a difficult matter in Ezra's reform: “Only Jonathan the son of Asahel and Jahaziah the son of Tikvah were employed about this matter: and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite helped them” (Ezra 10:15). His most important appearance is on the day the law was read aloud at the water gate: “Also Jeshua, and Bani, and Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodijah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the Levites, caused the people to understand the law: and the people stood in their place” (Nehemiah 8:7). The next verse states the method: “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Nehemiah 8:8). Later he is given standing oversight: “And Shabbethai and Jozabad, of the chief of the Levites, had the oversight of the outward business of the house of God” (Nehemiah 11:16). A man whose name means sabbath spent his life making the word of God plain to people who had come home from exile unable to read it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Shabbethai; the name is formed from the Hebrew for sabbath, and belongs to a Levite of Ezra's and Nehemiah's time.
webster_full: SHABBETHAI, n. A Levite who assisted in expounding the law to the people; from the Hebrew for sabbath.
EXPOUND, v.t. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret.
DISTINCTLY, adv. With distinctness; not confusedly; clearly; plainly; without ambiguity.
SENSE, n. Meaning; import; signification; the meaning of a word or phrase.
OVERSIGHT, n. Superintendence; watchful care; the charge and management of a business.
scriptures: Only Jonathan the son of Asahel and Jahaziah the son of Tikvah were employed about this matter: and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite helped them.

Also Jeshua, and Bani, and Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodijah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the Levites, caused the people to understand the law: and the people stood in their place.
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
And Shabbethai and Jozabad, of the chief of the Levites, had the oversight of the outward business of the house of God.
corruption_summary: Preaching is reconceived as inspiration, performance or application detached from the text, when Nehemiah 8 defines it as reading distinctly, giving the sense, and causing the people to understand.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the definition of exposition Nehemiah 8:8 supplies in a single verse. They read in the book in the law of God distinctly — the text itself, audibly and clearly; and gave the sense — what it means, since the people had been in Babylon and the Hebrew needed opening; and caused them to understand the reading — the aim is comprehension in the hearer, not admiration of the speaker. Shabbethai and thirteen named Levites did this among a congregation that stood in their place from morning until midday.

Every departure from that pattern is a recognisable failure of the modern pulpit. A sermon that never reads the text distinctly has replaced the word with the preacher. One that reads but never gives the sense leaves the hearer where Ezra's congregation was, with a book in a language they cannot follow. One that gives the sense but does not aim at understanding has become a lecture. The Reformers rebuilt the church's worship around this verse's logic, which is why a Reformed service is built around the reading and preaching of Scripture, and why the sermon ends in application rather than in applause.

pos: n. (an ancestor of a wall-builder, a sealer of the covenant, and a father of the king's officer)
etymology: Hebrew Mesheyzabel, meaning God delivers or God sets free. The name appears three times in Nehemiah, each in a different kind of service.
biblical_def: The name first appears in the roll of those who rebuilt Jerusalem's wall: “And next unto them repaired Meremoth the son of Urijah, the son of Koz. And next unto them repaired Meshullam the son of Berechiah, the son of Meshezabeel. And next unto them repaired Zadok the son of Baana” (Nehemiah 3:4). It appears again among the chiefs who set their seal to the covenant after the reading of the law: “Meshezabeel, Zadok, Jaddua” (Nehemiah 10:21). And a third time as the father of a man given a specific civil charge: “And Pethahiah the son of Meshezabeel, of the children of Zerah the son of Judah, was at the king's hand in all matters concerning the people” (Nehemiah 11:24). The covenant those chiefs sealed was not a vague resolution; it had terms: “They clave to their brethren, their nobles, and entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God's law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord, and his judgments and his statutes” (Nehemiah 10:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Meshezabeel; the Hebrew signifies God delivers, and the name occurs three times in Nehemiah.
webster_full: MESHEZABEEL, n. A man named in Nehemiah; in Hebrew, God delivers or sets free.
SEAL, v.t. To fasten with a seal; to ratify; to confirm; to settle or establish.
COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or forbear some act.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
SUBSCRIBE, v.t. To sign with one's own hand; to attest by writing the name beneath.
scriptures: And next unto them repaired Meremoth the son of Urijah, the son of Koz. And next unto them repaired Meshullam the son of Berechiah, the son of Meshezabeel. And next unto them repaired Zadok the son of Baana.
And Pethahiah the son of Meshezabeel, of the children of Zerah the son of Judah, was at the king's hand in all matters concerning the people.

They clave to their brethren, their nobles, and entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God's law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord, and his judgments and his statutes;
corruption_summary: Covenant renewal is reduced to a feeling of recommitment, when Nehemiah's congregation wrote names on a document and bound themselves under an oath with specified terms.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the concreteness of covenanting. After the law was read and the people wept and then feasted, they made a sure covenant, wrote it, and sealed it, and Nehemiah records eighty-four names of those who sealed — priests, Levites, and chiefs of the people, Meshezabeel among them. The terms were spelled out: no intermarriage with the peoples of the land, no trading on the sabbath, the seventh-year release, a temple tax, firstfruits, tithes. Nothing was left to sentiment.

This is the pattern behind the Reformed churches' practice of confession and subscription. A church that states what it believes in writing, and asks its officers to own it by name, is doing what Nehemiah 10 did. The objection that such documents quench the Spirit misreads both the chapter and the history: the covenant was made on the day the people had understood the words declared unto them, and their joy is recorded in the same paragraph as their oath. Where the terms are unwritten, the renewal cannot be kept, because no one can say afterwards what was promised.

pos: n. (head of one of the largest families to return from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Pachath Moab, literally governor of Moab — a title turned into a family name, probably from an ancestor who had held office in that territory.
biblical_def: The family is among the largest in the register of the return: “The children of Pahathmoab, of the children of Jeshua and Joab, two thousand eight hundred and twelve” (Ezra 2:6). A second company came up with Ezra himself years later: “Of the sons of Pahathmoab; Elihoenai the son of Zerahiah, and with him two hundred males” (Ezra 8:4). But the same house appears in the painful list of those who had taken foreign wives: “And of the sons of Pahathmoab; Adna, and Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezaleel, and Binnui, and Manasseh” (Ezra 10:30). And the house is on the wall in Nehemiah's day: “Malchijah the son of Harim, and Hashub the son of Pahathmoab, repaired the other piece, and the tower of the furnaces” (Nehemiah 3:11). Three thousand people, a repaired tower, and a column of names under discipline — the record of one family across two generations, kept without flattery and without concealment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Pahath-moab; the Hebrew signifies governor of Moab, and the name heads a large family of the return.
webster_full: PAHATH-MOAB, n. The head of a great family among the returning exiles; in Hebrew, governor of Moab.
EXILE, n. The state of being banished from one's country; the person banished.
RETURN, n. The act of coming back to the same place or state; restoration.
DISCIPLINE, n. Correction; chastisement; punishment intended to correct crimes or errors.
TOWER, n. A building, either round or square, raised to a considerable elevation, for defence or ornament.
scriptures: The children of Pahathmoab, of the children of Jeshua and Joab, two thousand eight hundred and twelve .
Of the sons of Pahathmoab; Elihoenai the son of Zerahiah, and with him two hundred males.
And of the sons of Pahathmoab; Adna, and Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezaleel, and Binnui, and Manasseh.
Malchijah the son of Harim, and Hashub the son of Pahathmoab, repaired the other piece, and the tower of the furnaces.
corruption_summary: Church discipline is treated as incompatible with grace, though Ezra names the offending households of the returned community and records the correction rather than suppressing it.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra 10 is a chapter modern readers find intolerable, and the difficulty deserves a straight answer rather than an evasion. The issue was not ethnicity; Ruth the Moabitess and Rahab the Canaanite are in the line of Christ, and the law provided for the stranger who joined himself to the LORD. The issue was the covenant, and specifically marriages contracted with the surrounding peoples in their idolatry, which was the very sin that had destroyed the northern kingdom and sent Judah to Babylon. The community had come home under a covenant and the households named had broken it.

The name itself faces no postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture records the failures of its best families without erasing their honours. The house of Pahath-moab returned nearly three thousand strong, sent another two hundred men with Ezra, and repaired the tower of the furnaces on the wall — and eight of its sons are listed by name among those who had to put away what they had taken. The same register holds both. A church willing to publish only one half of that account will end with neither honest discipline nor honest praise.

pos: n. (head of a family of the return, and a sealer of the covenant)
etymology: Hebrew Zattu, of uncertain meaning. The name heads a family counted twice in the registers of the return, with a discrepancy between the two counts that has its own lesson.
biblical_def: Ezra numbers the family at one figure: “The children of Zattu, nine hundred forty and five” (Ezra 2:8). Nehemiah, copying a register of the same return, gives another: “The children of Zattu, eight hundred forty and five” (Nehemiah 7:13). The house also appears among those whose sons had married foreign wives: “And of the sons of Zattu; Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, and Jeremoth, and Zabad, and Aziza” (Ezra 10:27). The family name also stands among the chiefs of the people who sealed the covenant to walk in God's law, written there in the variant form Zatthu. Such registers are the bookkeeping of a restored people, kept because God had promised a return and the returning had to be recorded.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Zattu; the name heads a family among the exiles who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel.
webster_full: ZATTU, n. The head of a family among those who returned from the Babylonish captivity.
REGISTER, n. A written account or entry of acts, judgments or proceedings; a book of record.
ENUMERATE, v.t. To count or tell number by number; to reckon or mention a number of things, each separately.
VARIANT, n. A different reading of a text; a form differing from another in some particular.
TRANSCRIBE, v.t. To copy; to write over again or in the same words; to write a copy of anything.
scriptures: The children of Zattu, nine hundred forty and five.
The children of Zattu, eight hundred forty and five.
And of the sons of Zattu; Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, and Jeremoth, and Zabad, and Aziza.

And my God put into mine heart to gather together the nobles, and the rulers, and the people, that they might be reckoned by genealogy. And I found a register of the genealogy of them which came up at the first, and found written therein,
corruption_summary: Numerical differences between parallel registers are offered as proof that Scripture errs, without regard for what the two documents are and what each of them claims.
corruption_paragraphs: The lists in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 differ in several totals, and this family is one of them — nine hundred forty and five against eight hundred forty and five. The difference is regularly produced as a plain contradiction. But Nehemiah states exactly what he is doing: he found a register of the genealogy of them which came up at the first, and copied it. Two documents about the same return, compiled at different points — one perhaps of those who enrolled to go and the other of those who actually arrived and settled — will differ, and honest transmission preserves both rather than harmonising them.

The name itself faces no postmodern redefinition. The dictionary's position on inerrancy is the confessional one: Scripture is without error in the original autographs, and the doctrine has never claimed that every numeral in every copy is free of scribal variation, or that two independent records of the same event must be verbally identical. What is asserted is that both registers are the word of God and that neither is teaching what a hostile reading requires them to teach. The chapter's actual subject is that God brought a people home and knew how many they were, family by family, to the last forty and five.
